title: Do heavy things fall faster?
intro: A short explainer video with two questions along the way.
transfer: Drop a flat and a crumpled sheet of paper at the same time: both weigh the same. Which one lands first, and why?

scenes.caption: A ball and a feather start falling at the same time. The ball lands first, the feather floats slowly down.
Is it because of the weight? No. The feather offers the air a lot of surface, and the air slows it down a lot. It hardly slows the ball.
Now we pump the air out of a tube. In a vacuum, the ball and the feather fall exactly equally fast.
Without air, all bodies fall equally fast, however heavy they are. Differences in everyday life come from the air.

questions.prompt: Why does the feather land later than the ball?
options: The air slows the feather down a lot
The feather is simply much lighter
Balls naturally fall a bit faster
questions.explanation: The difference comes from air resistance. Without air the feather would be just as fast.

questions.prompt: What happens to the ball and the feather without air?
options: The ball falls a little faster
questions.explanation: In a vacuum nothing slows them down. Then all bodies fall equally fast, however heavy.

title: Why does everything fall at the same speed?
intro: Explain to the AI why, without air, a heavy and a light body fall equally fast.
transfer: When someone says “heavy things fall faster”, ask back: is it the weight or the air?

content.goal: You explain in your own words why mass plays no role without air and where differences in everyday life come from.
content.aiRole: You are a physics learning coach. The learner should explain in their own words why all bodies fall equally fast without air and why there are still differences in everyday life. Use the three experiments in the material. Do not explain it yourself; ask instead: what is the same in experiment 2, and what is different? So what can it not be? What is missing in experiment 3? A learner who is further along may think about why the greater pull on the heavy ball is balanced by its greater inertia, but do not require it. Do not give a finished explanation. If an answer is wrong (for example “heavy things fall faster”), ask a follow-up question using one of the experiments. One question at a time, at most 2 to 3 short sentences. Finally, ask for an explanation in two sentences: one about mass, one about air.
content.opening: Look at experiment 2: both sheets weigh the same. Why does the crumpled one still land first?

material.title: Three experiments (made up)
lines: Experiment 1: Two balls of the same size, one weighs 1 kg, the other 100 g. Dropped from 2 m, both land almost at the same time.
Experiment 2: A flat and a crumpled sheet of paper fall. The crumpled one lands first.
Experiment 3: In a tube with no air, a coin and a feather fall equally fast.

criteria.label: Mass plays no role
criteria.hint: Without air, does the fall time depend on the weight?

criteria.label: Air resistance
criteria.hint: What slows down the flat sheet and the feather?

fallbackReplies: Interesting. If both sheets weigh the same: what else can make one of them fall faster?
Now look at experiment 3. What is missing in the tube, and what does that mean for the coin and the feather?
And experiment 1: the balls are the same size but different weights. What does that tell you about mass?
Now explain it in two sentences: one about mass, one about air.
Thanks, that is an explanation in your own words. You can finish the lesson now.
